title: Movie Executive
protagonist: Rebecca Buckley, studio production and acquisitions executive
primary_metric: projected opening-weekend box office revenue per dollar of production budget

options.A: Produce Waves In The Tales (rigorous stratified random phone survey of real customers, n=87 nationally / n=15 in the presented 13-30 stratum, $64,300,000 budget)
options.B: Produce The Flower's Ice (huge theater-goer convenience sample, 835 approached / 23 usable responses, $102,900,000 budget)

legacy_conversion_note: Source: 'Case Study_ Movie Executive.docx' + 'Guide Notes.docx' (source/Y1/Session 5/Movie Producer). The original offered THREE screenplay options (Waves In The Tales, The Gate Of The Future, The Flower's Ice); per the human-approved lock in cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md's 'movie-producer' entry, The Gate Of The Future is dropped as the weakest/most methodologically compromised of the three (its own survey -- 46 movie critics emailed, 23 replies -- is not a customer-facing test at all), leaving the two locked options A/B used here. The original screenplay concepts were attributed to real, still-working filmmakers (e.g. 'an original screenplay concept by Quentin Tarantino') as a flavor device; this conversion replaces those with fictional screenwriter names (Marisol Kane, Desmond Vail) since attaching invented, sometimes-mocked plot loglines to real people's names serves no mathematical purpose and is an unnecessary personality-rights/taste risk. Each film's original survey APPENDIX table (the actual scatter of individual respondent scores) was not machine-readable in the source .docx -- almost certainly a table or image the text extraction did not capture, the same class of gap documented for Archery Camp's Appendix B. This conversion designs its own clean, internally-consistent survey dataset for each film (Appendix A/B), preserving every real, stated fact from the source text -- sample sizes (87 phone / 15 shown for Waves, 835 approached / 23 usable for Flower's Ice), sampling methods (stratified random vs. convenience), production budgets ($64,300,000 / $102,900,000), genres, and ratings -- and is NOT claiming the individual respondent rows are the original film's real archived data; only the case's own designed rows are fictional. Waves' 'Gate Of The Future' sibling budget ($37,600,000) and its dropped survey are not carried into this case. The primary metric (revenue per production dollar, rather than the original's separately-listed 'estimated Total Box Office revenue' and 'marketing spend' asks) was chosen to give the case a single comparable decision metric per SPEC §2's balance test while still producing both of the original Challenge's required numbers (D5 revenue, D6 marketing budget) as intermediate/parallel deliverables. new_coverage[] is empty: every Statistics-and-Probability sampling/scatter-plot/correlation skill this case's deliverables genuinely force (scatter plot, line of best fit, correlation, slope, sample/population/sampling-method vocabulary, mean, percent, decimal operations) already has n>0 in the spine from prior cases (e.g. Acton Survey, Medical Statician, Cardiology) -- there is no adjacent uncovered skill in this group the case's real math reaches, so this is the legacy-conversion carve-out (2026-08-13 doctrine amendment), not padding.

sources.claim: Average U.S. movie theater ticket price nationally
sources.org: National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO, now Cinema United)
sources.title: NATO 2022 annual ticket-price estimate, as reported in "Finally, the NATO Report Tells Us the Average Price of a Movie Theater Ticket"
sources.note: NATO's own annual-report estimate, the first the trade group had released in three years at time of publication (March 2023); up 15% from $9.16 in 2019. No more recent NATO/Cinema United figure could be independently confirmed as of this case's research date -- used in Appendix D as real-world pricing context, not as a load-bearing input to the revenue projection itself (the case's projected ticket prices in D4/D5 come from the survey data, not this figure).

sources.claim: Marketing (P&A) budget can equal or exceed a film's production budget; named examples span roughly 1.1x-4x production cost, and a wide release typically needs to earn about twice its production budget to cover production plus marketing/distribution before profit
sources.value: Named examples (e.g. $15,000 production/$18M P&A; $22M production/$25-35M P&A) plus a general 'earn ~2x production budget' breakeven rule of thumb
sources.title: P&A Explained: The Film Budget Bigger Than Production
sources.note: Industry guide, not a primary trade body; gives named examples and a breakeven-multiple rule of thumb, not a '20-30% of production budget' marketing-share figure. The case's own 20-30%-of-production-budget marketing guidance (used in D6) is a separate, author-stated planning estimate, not a number taken directly from this source -- corrected 2026-08-20 after a data-decay check found the article does not state that figure.

sources.claim: Statistical correction/weighting of a nonprobability (convenience) sample removes only part of its selection bias, not all of it
sources.value: Best-performing weighting method reduced average estimated bias from 8.4 to 6.0 percentage points across 24 benchmarks (roughly 30% of the bias corrected, ~70% remaining)
sources.units: percentage points of bias, across 24 benchmark comparisons
sources.title: Reducing Bias on Benchmarks (For Weighting Online Opt-In Samples, What Matters Most?)
sources.note: Studies online opt-in panels specifically, not in-person theater-lobby convenience samples -- but is the best available real research on how much of a convenience/nonprobability sample's bias statistical correction can actually recover, which is the general, transferable principle FACILITATOR.md's Twist applies to The Flower's Ice's convenience-sampled 'excess' enthusiasm. Not cited in case.md; used only in the facilitator-only Twist per SPEC's discussion-reveal doctrine (SPEC §7.2). The 8.4-to-6.0-point, 24-benchmark figure comes from this 2018 report, not Pew's earlier 2016 'Evaluating Online Nonprobability Surveys' report, which studies a different set of benchmarks and does not contain this figure.

modeling_assumptions.text: National addressable opening-weekend audience for a wide release in this genre is assumed at 8,000,000 people. No public source states a genre-specific addressable audience for a fictional film concept; this is a stated scenario assumption, not a sourced figure. It scales both films' projected revenue equally and does not by itself determine which film wins on revenue-per-production-dollar.

deliverables.text: A scatter plot, with a line of best fit drawn on it, of each film's test-audience survey data (Appendix A and Appendix B).
For each film: a written classification of the scatter plot's correlation, an estimated correlation coefficient, and the line of best fit's equation (slope and y-intercept).
A table stating the statistical population, sample size analyzed, and sampling method for each film's survey, plus a judgment of which is more likely to generalize to real opening-weekend moviegoers.
For each film, the share of respondents scoring 9-10 on likelihood-to-see (the 'definite buyers') and their mean willingness-to-pay price.
A projected opening-weekend box office revenue for each film, built from D4's numbers and Appendix E's addressable-audience assumption.
A revenue-per-production-dollar comparison table for both films, plus a recommended marketing budget for the chosen film using Appendix D's sourced guidance, and a final recommendation.

twist.alt_convention_note: Alternate, equally defensible convention: apply the 30% retained-fraction directly to the dollar gap between the two films' projected revenues instead of to the top-2-box rate gap. Winner is unchanged under either convention; only the exact post-twist margin differs (36.0% vs 42.6%).

balance.argument_a: Waves In The Tales is the smallest, cheapest concept on the table ($64.3M), but its survey signal is almost perfectly linear (r=0.97) -- a small, trustworthy dataset gathered by stratified random sampling that reliably represents the customer population it was drawn from. 26.67% of its 13-30 stratum are 'definite buyers' (score 9-10), willing to pay an average of $8.00. Because random/stratified sampling generalizes, that rate is more defensible as a real opening-weekend prediction than a bigger but methodologically weaker number. Its projected revenue-per-production-dollar (26.54 cents per dollar) leads Flower's Ice.
balance.argument_b: The Flower's Ice was tested against a vastly larger pool -- 835 people approached, not 87 -- and even in its 23-response usable sample, a higher share (34.78%) score as definite buyers, willing to pay a higher average price ($8.625) than Waves' definite buyers. Even though the sampling method is a convenience sample and may not generalize as cleanly (r=0.80, noisier than Waves), the sheer scale of enthusiasm nearly closes the revenue-per-dollar gap (23.32 cents per dollar vs. Waves' 26.54) despite costing 60% more to produce -- and its raw projected dollar total ($24.0M vs. $17.1M) is larger in absolute terms.
balance.margin_basis: primary_metric = (top-2-box fraction x mean willingness-to-pay price x MA1 addressable audience) / production budget, computed independently for each film from Appendix A/B's survey data and Appendix E's stated assumption; margin = (higher ratio - lower ratio) / lower ratio.

sensitivity_note: The case's revenue-per-production-dollar verdict is intentionally insensitive to the size of Appendix E's national addressable-audience assumption, since that figure scales both films' projected revenue equally and cancels out of the ratio between them. What genuinely drives the (thin, 13.8%) margin is each film's own survey-derived definite-buyer rate and price, weighed against its own budget -- and FACILITATOR.md's Twist shows that a real, sourced statistical-correction principle (Pew Research on nonprobability-sample bias) can move that margin from thin to decisive without changing which option wins.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; the 'deep conflict' threads (sample size vs. sample quality; raw revenue vs. revenue-per-dollar) drop to one thread instead of two; runtime shortens proportionally.
